title: George McCollum, Shots and Wooden Joe compared
summary: Miller describes McCollum as a classical player and compares Shots, Buddy and Wooden Joe as lead or Armstrong-style players.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. What about George McCollum? What kind of trumpet player was he?
He's pretty good on straight music. I don't mean straight music, but classic. He played a little jump-up stuff. He played most of this.
I believe that might be... It looks mighty dark, I mean, I believe that's what it is.
Yeah, you want to wash it out or something?
No, I got something out there, I'll see what it is.
Okay, well let's turn the machine off again for a second.

You never noticed how he played? Two of them, I never noticed them. All I noticed, one of them was more like Buddy and one of them was like Lewis. That's Shot, he was the one of the order of Lewis, you know, trying to play like Lewis. And Woodenhead Joe, I said, no, I didn't play much tennis. What is his name? Wooden Joe.
Well he was more of a straight man, wouldn't you? He played more lead. Yeah. It was hot, but it was lead. Yeah. Now Shot's played a lot of second, huh?
Played a lot of stuff like bunk, but he had more push than bunk in the old days, and fire. No. Struck me. Don't you think so? What, huh? Don't you think so? Don't you think so?
Don't you think he had, you know, more fire than bunk?
Yeah, more fire. Yeah. I don't think he had more fire than bunk. Yeah, more fire. Yeah.
